title: The name at sea
eyebrow: Lloyd's List, 1865–1878 · and an old Cardiff family
dek: Findmypast's newspaper archive returns seventy articles for «Defranceschi». The earliest sixty are not about people at all. They are shipping intelligence — the daily columns of vessel movements that Lloyd's List and the Shipping and Mercantile Gazette printed for the insurance market — and in them, for thirteen years, a master of this name is at sea.
how: **How to read these columns.** They give the vessel, then the master's surname, then a port: «Aquilone, Defranceschi, Newcastle». No forename, ever. So what follows is **the shape of a career, not the identity of a man** — it could be one master across four ships, or a family of them. This page will not pretend to know which.

rows.t: The Black Sea grain trade. Cleared **Constantinople** for the United Kingdom in October 1865 and appears in the Gazette's Constantinople and **Galatz** columns through November and December — Galatz being the Danube grain port. In November 1866 she is at **Marseilles, arrived from Balchik** on the Bulgarian coast.

«**Trieste, April 21 — Peppina Luigia, Defranceschi, Troon**», in the Edinburgh Evening Courant of 28 April 1869, and in the Exchange Shipping List «at **Trieste from Troon**». Troon is the Ayrshire coal port. Trieste out, Scottish coal home.

«**Rassel, Defranceschi, at Dardanelles Oct 13**» (December 1869); «**Antwerp, arrived Jan. 14 … Rachel, Defranceschi, Odessa**» (January 1870); and in August 1870 «**Constantinople, cleared Aug. 6 for … Rachel, Defranceschi, United Kingdom**». Odessa wheat to the Low Countries.

The one the record follows properly, and the one with a tonnage: **«Aquilone, Aus, 350, Defranceschi»** — Austrian, three hundred and fifty tons. The Belfast Telegraph calls her «**the Austrian barque Aquilone**» in July 1872 and «**the Italian barque Aquillone**» three weeks later, which is a fair summary of what Istria was.

voyages.heading: The Aquilone, port by port
voyages.lead: Assembled from Lloyd's List, the Shipping and Mercantile Gazette, the Belfast Telegraph, the Shields Daily Gazette, the Western Morning News, the South Wales Daily News and the Cardiff Shipping and Mercantile Gazette. Every line is a printed sighting.

passed down the Dardanelles, for Falmouth

company.heading: And look who else is in the column
company.text:
Shipping intelligence lists masters together, and the names printed beside Defranceschi in the Constantinople and Galatz columns of 1865 are these: **Bujanovich · Lacovich · Riedyk · Baccarcich · Cattarinich · Ivancich · Nicolich · Marecich · Garanovich · Milossevich · Lusina · Soich · Marusich · Minach**.

That is not a random sample of the world's shipmasters. **It is the Austro-Hungarian merchant marine of the eastern Adriatic** — the sea-captain families of **Lošinj, Rijeka, Bakar, Dubrovnik and the Bocche**, who carried Black Sea grain to the west and British coal home for two generations.

This archive has an unplaced household of the surname at **Bakar** — twelve people across three generations, styled **Dominus**, citizen class, from before 1772 to a death in 1819 — and has never been able to say what they were. **Bakar was a shipowning town with a nautical academy.** A Defranceschi master in the Austrian fleet in the 1860s and 70s is not proof of anything about them. It is the right sea, the right flag and the right company, and it is written down here so that the next person to open the Bakar registers knows to look for a captain.

cardiff.heading: An old Cardiff family, and a girl from the Vienna Conservatoire
cardiff.lead: The Aquilone entered outward at Cardiff for Guadaloupe on 11 December 1877. Nineteen years later the Cardiff papers carry the surname again, and not in the shipping columns.

rows.q: **CARDIFF EXHIBITION. ADDITIONAL ATTRACTION.** Messrs Thompson and Shackell have arranged with **Signorina Defranceschi** to give a series of pianoforte recitals on Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday afternoons in the Art Gallery **on a magnificent harpsichord grand**.

This piano is a fac-simile of the instrument presented to the Duchess of York on the occasion of her marriage. **Signorina Defranceschi belongs to an old Cardiff family, and has recently taken her degree at the Vienna Conservatoire of Music.** The first recital…
rows.why:
**«An old Cardiff family.»** In 1896 a Cardiff paper could write that phrase about people of this surname and expect its readers to know who was meant.

And there is a marriage to go with it. Findmypast's **Wales Roman Catholic Marriages** has **Emerico de Franceschi, married 1876 at St Peter's, Roath, Glamorganshire** — the Catholic parish of Cardiff, in the year before the Aquilone cleared the Bute Docks for the West Indies. The transcript is outside this subscription's tier and has not been read.

rows.lab: South Wales Echo, 1 June 1896 — «The Man About Town»
rows.q: …in a picture gallery, but **one might go far and not meet with such a finished pianist as I heard on Saturday**. Signorina Defranceschi, who was giving a pianoforte recital free to the visitors to the Exhibition, is a young lady who has **passed with distinction**…
rows.why: A columnist wandering the Cardiff Exhibition, stopping in front of a harpsichord, and going home to write that he had not expected to hear playing like that. It is the only sentence in this whole archive in which somebody of the name is simply **admired**.

honest: **What this is and is not.** Shipping intelligence gives a surname and no more, so no man on this page is identified — not the master of the *Natalia* in the Black Sea in 1865, not the master of the *Aquilone* at Cardiff in 1877, and not the family the *South Wales Echo* called old. **None of them is connected to any line on this site**, and the surname is a patronymic that formed independently wherever Francesco was a common name. What the seventy articles do establish is that between 1865 and 1878 the name was on the master's line of Austrian ships in the Black Sea, the Adriatic and the Bristol Channel, and that by the 1890s there were Defranceschi in Cardiff long enough established to be called old. **Both are new to this archive.**
source: Findmypast British & Irish Newspapers, keyword search on the name, 9 September 2026: 70 articles. Titles cited — Lloyd's List; Shipping and Mercantile Gazette; Cardiff Shipping and Mercantile Gazette; Belfast Telegraph; Shields Daily Gazette; Western Morning News; Edinburgh Evening Courant; South Wales Daily News; South Wales Echo; Shields Daily News; Daily Malta Chronicle and Garrison Gazette. A second search on «de Franceschi» returned a further 83 articles, and those readings are included here. OCR is imperfect and the vessel's name is variously set as Aquilone, Aquillone, Aquions, Aqalone and Aquilooe; readings here follow the clearest setting of each line. Lloyd's Register of Shipping for 1875 and 1877–78 searched in full text from the Internet Archive's scans of the Lloyd's Register Foundation copies (items HECROS1875, HECROS1877): no Aquilone in either.

rows.lab: The loss of the Shields steamer «Aberlady Bay», Board of Trade inquiry, June 1889
rows.q: George Howard Davidson, second officer; Peter Engstrom, A.B.; **George De Franceschi, A.B., an Austrian**; and Edward Eliassen, A.B., all stated that the light which was observed on the port bow of the vessel…
rows.why:
*Shields Daily News*, 22 June 1889. Not a master this time — an **able seaman**, giving evidence at the Board of Trade inquiry into a wreck, and the reporter takes the trouble to write **«an Austrian»** after his name.

This is the other half of the same world. The Adriatic did not only send captains into the British trades; it sent crews. **George De Franceschi, A.B.**, is the first man of this surname anywhere in this archive who is named, dated, placed on a named ship, and quoted.

rows.q: PASSENGERS ARRIVED ON THE 11th. By the **Aust[ro]-Hung[arian] Carola from Syracuse**: Rev. H. H. Mitchell, **E. De Franceschi**, L. Miceli and family, G. S. Cala…
rows.why: *Daily Malta Chronicle and Garrison Gazette*, 13 October 1899. Twenty-one years after the *Aquilone* last appeared, somebody of the name is still crossing the middle sea under the Habsburg flag — this time as a passenger, on the Austro-Hungarian Lloyd's *Carola* out of Syracuse.

rows.lab: Sydney, 6 January 1893 — and the Australian mystery closes
rows.q:
**INWARD.** A LIST of the Crew and Passengers arrived in the Ship **Miowera** of **London**, **James Stott** Master, of the Burthen of **1,911 Tons**, from the Port of **Melbourne** to **Sydney**, New South Wales, 1893.

SEAMEN'S NAMES · Station · Age · Of What Nation
… Alex. McKinnon · **Q.M.** · 45 · —
… P. Nicholson · ″ · 36 · —
… **G. Defranceschi · ″ · 28 · Austrian**
rows.why:
For two days this archive has carried an unexplained line: **«G de Franceschi, born 1865, New South Wales, 1893»** — one Australian record fifty-seven years before every other, in the decade this family's own branch was moving down to the Kvarner, in the country the line eventually reaches. It was queued twice as a lead to chase.

**It is not a migrant. He is crew.** The index field «Seaman or passenger» reads **Seamen**, and the station column, dittoed down from Alex McKinnon above him, reads **Q.M. — Quartermaster**. Twenty-eight years old, **Austrian**, at the wheel of a brand-new 1,911-ton Huddart Parker steamer on the overnight run from Melbourne to Sydney, on the sixth of January 1893.

He was not going to Australia. He was **passing through it**, the way the master of the *Aquilone* passed through Cardiff and George De Franceschi passed through the Tyne. **The lead is closed, and the answer is better than the question**: the surname reaches Australia in 1893 not as a settler but as a sailor, and does not settle there for another fifty-seven years.

registry.heading: Where the Aquilone was registered — and why London cannot say

rows.lab: She is not in Lloyd's Register
rows.text:
The obvious next question is her port of registry, because that is the one fact that would tell us whether the *Aquilone* was a **Bakar**, **Rijeka** or **Lošinj** ship. Lloyd's Register is the book that answers such questions, and its volumes are digitised.

**The full text of Lloyd's Register for 1875 and for 1877–78 was downloaded and searched. There is no Aquilone in either.** The only near miss is the French *Aquilon*, of Jersey, 48 tons.

That is not a failure; it is the answer. **Lloyd's classed British ships and those foreign ships whose owners paid to be classed by London.** An Austrian barque of 350 tons working the Levant grain trade and the Bristol Channel coal trade had no need of it: she would have been on the register of the **Austro-Hungarian Veritas**, and her papers are in **Trieste and Rijeka**, not in Cornhill.

**So the port of registry is a question for the Austrian register, and this archive now knows to ask it there.**

Two things the British press supplies that the Austrian register would confirm. Her **tonnage**: 350 in the Cardiff Shipping and Mercantile Gazette of 17 December 1877, 351 in the Shipping and Mercantile Gazette of 7 June 1878 — the small discrepancy between gross and net that every ship of that period carries. And her **Cardiff agent**: «Aquilone, Aus, 350, Defranceschi, **G. Montaldo & Co**». Montaldo was one of the Italian shipping houses of the Bute Docks. A firm's ledgers are a better finding aid than a ship's name.

places.heading: And the village names, tested against a hundred million pages

rows.text: Not one article in the entire British and Irish newspaper archive mentions this family's village by name. **Zero.** Gračišće existed for the British press exactly as much as it existed for the clerk who wrote «Frieste» on Joseph's draft card.

rows.lab: «Pisino» — nine hundred and fifteen, and all of them junk
rows.text: The optical character reader turns «early rising» into «TARLY PISINO» and there was a brand of stove polish called **Pisino Sun**. Nine hundred and fifteen results, not one about Pazin. It is a useful reminder of what a keyword search in an OCR archive is actually doing.

rows.lab: «Buccari» — one thousand three hundred and seventy-seven, and all of them shipping
rows.text:
**Bakar had its own standing heading in the London shipping press.** «**BUCCARI. Arrived [March 5] from — Carl Emma, Holz, Trieste**» (Shipping and Mercantile Gazette, 21 March 1850). «**BUCCARI. Mima, Bachich (Sept 2) Antwerp**» (16 November 1869). Column after column, decade after decade, between Cagliari and Carloforte in the alphabetical run of ports.

The town where this archive has twelve unplaced people of the surname, styled *Dominus*, was a port the London insurance market tracked **daily, by name, for a century**.

**And no Defranceschi ever appears under that heading.** A combined search — the surname and the port — returns nothing. Whatever the Bakar household were, they were not clearing ships out of Bakar under their own name in the years the British press was watching.
